profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting at a mid-sized SaaS company preparing a 6-week internal case study on CI practice monitoring across three product groups. The Developer Experience team has built a telemetry pipeline that extracts GitHub Actions and Jenkins signals, while Engineering Operations is assembling a dashboard and narrative for directors to review whether CI monitoring improves visibility, communication, and perceived software quality. The agenda is to align on the interface between the telemetry export and the reporting dashboard, confirm what will be included in the first weekly rollout, and clarify handoffs for status updates and shared artifacts. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on what data will be delivered each week, how teams will be compared to a baseline, and who will update the central dashboard for the pilot.

members.name: Camila Rocha
members.expertise: CI/CD infrastructure, GitHub Actions instrumentation, build telemetry, internal developer platforms
members.background: Camila leads the platform workstream that added monitoring hooks to the company's CI services and has recently migrated several teams from Jenkins to GitHub Actions while keeping legacy jobs alive for release branches.
members.private_state: She wants the pilot to look operationally smooth with minimal manual reporting overhead, and she is worried that leadership-facing metrics will be questioned if they include noisy legacy or optional jobs that her team does not actively control.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'baseline' for CI monitoring, they usually mean a rolling 30-day pre-change benchmark generated automatically from the telemetry store.
A 'pipeline failure' should mean failure in required build-and-test checks that gate merges, not failures in optional nightly, security, or release-maintenance workflows.
A 'weekly feed' should come from the existing automated BigQuery export that refreshes every Monday morning UTC, because manual files are not realistic to maintain.
The 'current workflow config' for a team is whatever is on the default branch, since that is what the telemetry parser reads by default.

members.name: Rafael Mendes
members.expertise: cross-team reporting, engineering health metrics, leadership reviews, process rollout coordination
members.background: Rafael coordinates engineering effectiveness initiatives and is responsible for consolidating survey results, interview notes, and operational metrics into a dashboard used by directors and team leads.
members.private_state: He wants the pilot dashboard to be easy for directors and team managers to consume without caveats, and he is concerned that inconsistencies across teams will make the case study look inconclusive unless the reporting package feels standardized and presentation-ready.
hidden_assumptions: When stakeholders say 'baseline,' they usually mean a fixed before-pilot snapshot from the April sprint review deck so later weekly changes can be compared to a stable point.
A 'pipeline failure' should cover any failed CI run visible to developers, because teams experience all of those failures as friction regardless of whether they gate merges.
A 'weekly feed' means a presentation-ready artifact, typically a cleaned CSV or sheet dropped into the shared reporting folder by Monday local business hours.
The 'current workflow config' for the pilot is the branch configuration teams are actually running for the release train, which for two pilot groups is the release branch rather than default.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to compare each team's CI metrics against 'the baseline.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means an automatically computed rolling 30-day benchmark immediately preceding each reporting week.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the fixed pre-pilot snapshot captured in the April engineering review materials.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see 'baseline' as standard reporting language and assume the organization already has one obvious reference point, so neither expects the term itself to need unpacking.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a pipeline failure
misalignment_points.surface_form: They align on tracking 'pipeline failures' for the pilot dashboard.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 counts only failed required CI checks that block merges on the main development path.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 counts any visible failed CI run affecting teams, including optional nightly jobs, flaky security scans, and release-maintenance workflows.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The shared goal of monitoring CI reliability makes 'pipeline failures' sound self-evident, and both assume the other is using the common-sense operational view without thinking about inclusion criteria.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Camila's team will send a 'weekly feed' for Rafael's dashboard update.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 plans to expose an automatically refreshed BigQuery table and assumes Rafael will pull from it directly.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects a cleaned CSV or spreadsheet placed in the shared reporting folder so he can merge it with survey and interview data.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The handoff is discussed as routine reporting plumbing, and 'weekly feed' sounds like a generic deliverable label that hides incompatible assumptions about the delivery mechanism.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss using 'the current workflow config' to annotate which CI practices each pilot team has enabled.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 refers to the workflow files on each repository's default branch because that is what her parser reads as the active source of truth.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 refers to the release-branch workflow configuration currently used by the two pilot teams shipping from stabilization branches.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both participants are referring to a real and legitimate 'current' configuration for the same repositories, and branch-specific operational reality is familiar enough that neither hears the phrase as ambiguous.

turns.inner_thought: The extraction jobs are finally stable across the three pilot groups, and I want to lock the handoff down in a way that doesn't create manual work for my team. If Rafael is expecting the usual weekly feed, he can just use the BigQuery export we already refresh on Mondays. As long as we keep this tied to the automated pipeline, I won't have to defend ad hoc spreadsheets later.
turns.utterance: I wanted to start with the telemetry side. The extraction is running for all three pilot groups now, so I mostly want to confirm the handoff into your dashboard and make sure we're aligned on the weekly feed.

turns.inner_thought: Good, if the data stream is live, I can shape the dashboard around a simple before-and-after story for directors. The key is keeping everything anchored to the baseline from the April sprint review deck so nobody asks why the reference point moves every week. If this looks standardized, the case study will feel credible.
turns.utterance: Perfect. From my side, the main goal is to show how each team is moving against the baseline so we have a clean story before the director review in six weeks.

turns.inner_thought: I can have the weekly feed available next Monday with no extra lift, since the export lands automatically after the Monday UTC refresh. And of course the baseline will stay sensible because the 30-day pre-week window will keep rolling forward as new telemetry comes in. That's the normal way to avoid one weird week skewing the trend.
turns.utterance: That works. I can expose the weekly feed starting next Monday, and the baseline should update cleanly once the telemetry window rolls forward, so the comparisons ought to stay pretty readable.

turns.inner_thought: Great, if Camila's team is sending the weekly feed, I can just drop it into the shared reporting folder and merge it with the survey and interview tabs. And keeping the April snapshot as the baseline will make the trend line much easier to explain in leadership review than something that shifts under us.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. Using the April snapshot as the baseline will make the trend story a lot easier for leadership, and I'll fold the weekly feed into the shared reporting folder on my side.

turns.inner_thought: Next I need to steer the metric conversation toward the signal I trust. For the dashboard, pipeline failures should mean the required build-and-test checks that actually gate merges; otherwise we'll drag in noisy optional runs my team doesn't control and leadership will question the whole set. If those required checks get quieter over the six weeks, that's a strong story.
turns.utterance: On the metric definitions, I do think we should include pipeline failures. That'll be especially useful for showing whether the required checks are getting less noisy over the course of the pilot.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, pipeline failures definitely belong in there because teams complain about all the failed runs they see, not just the ones that block a merge. The interview notes from support keep calling out broken nightly jobs and security scans as part of the friction story, so this metric can tie the operational data to what people are reporting qualitatively.
turns.utterance: Agreed. Pipeline failures will help a lot, especially since the support teams keep bringing up broken nightly and security runs in the interviews.

turns.inner_thought: I should also make sure the practice annotations come straight from the parser path we already support. The simplest thing is to read the current workflow config from each repo's default branch at export time, since that's what the telemetry parser treats as the source of truth. I really don't want to invent branch-specific exceptions during the pilot.
turns.utterance: The other piece I'll add is an annotation of which CI practices each pilot team has enabled. I can read the current workflow config from each repository when the export runs and attach that to the dataset.

turns.inner_thought: That should solve one of my presentation headaches. For Mobile API and Billing, what matters is the release-branch setup they're actually operating on right now, so if the current workflow config reflects that, then the dashboard notes will line up with what team leads expect to see. Good, that keeps the narrative consistent.
turns.utterance: That should help a lot. Mobile API and Billing are still on their release-branch setup, so having the current workflow config called out will match what those teams are seeing day to day.

turns.inner_thought: I should close the loop on the operational cadence so nobody asks my team for a manual send. The export table refreshes early Monday UTC, and Rafael can just pick up the weekly feed from there. As long as he pulls from the table, this stays low-touch and repeatable.
turns.utterance: So to summarize from my side: we'll keep the automated export stable, and you can pick up the weekly feed once the table refreshes early Monday UTC.

turns.inner_thought: Great, then I can plan to update the dashboard Monday afternoon once the file lands in the shared folder and compare the latest numbers back to the fixed baseline for the memo. If I keep the package clean and on schedule, directors will treat this like a polished reporting stream rather than a pilot with caveats.
